teaching.causalExplanation: Start with what the poster gets right, because a good analysis justifies the choices as well as finding faults. Justifying means saying why each graph suits its data, not just naming it. The big number shows one key fact, the share of students getting eight hours or more, seven of twenty. One number deserves one big, clear tile. The sector graph shows where phones charge. Those four places make one whole, a hundred per cent, and a sector graph is built for parts of one whole. The phone row uses one icon per student, so twelve of twenty is visible at a glance. And a column graph is the right choice to compare two groups, phone in the bedroom against phone elsewhere. Each graph was chosen for its data. Now the column graph's problem. Its vertical axis starts at six hours, not at nought. The bedroom group averaged six point six hours, so its column rises just nought point six above the base. The other group averaged eight point one, two point one above the base. On the page, one column is three and a half times as tall as the other. Slide the axis back to nought, and the truth appears. Six point six against eight point one. The elsewhere group's average is about a quarter more, an extra one and a half hours. That's a real difference, worth reporting. But the cut-off axis made it look like the bedroom group sleeps less than a third as much, which is false. The truncated axis is the most common trick, but there are others. Pictures can lie with area. To show twice as many phones, someone draws a phone twice as tall. But to keep its shape, it's twice as wide too, so it covers four times the space, and the eye sees four times as much. Three D sector graphs tilt the circle, so the slices at the front look bigger than they are. Scales with uneven steps squash some changes and stretch others. A line graph can start and stop at handy dates, and hide the rest. And a percentage needs its sample size. Thirty-five per cent sounds solid, until you ask, of how many? Here, it's seven students out of twenty.

scenes.teachingReason: Even an honest graph has limits, and conclusions and predictions have to respect them. Our graphs describe twenty Year 11 students, at one school, on one night. They can't tell us about all teenagers, or about every night. Our data came from an observational study, so they can't show that phones cause less sleep. An average hides the spread. Behind six point six hours is one student who slept just three. And no graph can safely predict outside its data. It can't tell us how next year's Year 11 will sleep. So here's a fair conclusion. In our sample of twenty Year 11 students on one school night, those whose phones charged outside the bedroom slept about one and a half hours more on average. That doesn't show the phone caused it, or that all teenagers are the same.
